title: Portal — Rendering Outside the Component Tree

subChunks.title: Portal — Rendering Outside the Component Tree
subChunks.hookHtml: Modals, tooltips, and dropdowns have a CSS problem: they need to appear above everything else, but if they're nested inside a component with overflow: hidden or a low z-index, they get clipped. React's createPortal lets you render a component's JSX into a different DOM node — typically document.body — while keeping it connected to the React component tree for state and event handling.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
The problem portals solve

<!-- The card has overflow:hidden -->
<div class="card" style="overflow: hidden; position: relative;">
  <!-- This modal is CLIPPED by the card's overflow -->
  <Modal />
</div>

Even with z-index: 9999, the modal is constrained by its ancestor's styles. The fix: render the modal directly in <body>.

createPortal

import { createPortal } from 'react-dom';

function Modal({ isOpen, onClose, children }) {
  if (!isOpen) return null;

  return createPortal(
    // JSX to render:
    <div className="modal-overlay" onClick={onClose}>
      <div className="modal-dialog" onClick={e => e.stopPropagation()}>
        {children}
        <button onClick={onClose}>Close</button>
      </div>
    </div>,

    // DOM target:
    document.body
  );
}

Key behaviours of portals

  • Events bubble through the React tree, not the DOM tree. A click inside the portal modal bubbles to the modal's React parent — even though the DOM parent is <body>
  • Context still works. Portals are still inside the React component tree for context purposes
  • The portal mounts/unmounts with its parent. When the Modal component unmounts, the portal content is removed

Creating a portal target

For production use, add a dedicated portal container to your HTML:

<!-- index.html -->
<div id="root"></div>
<div id="portal"></div>  <!-- Add this -->
// Modal.jsx
const portalEl = document.getElementById('portal');

return createPortal(<div className="modal">{children}</div>, portalEl);

Vex: "A portal escapes the DOM hierarchy but stays in the React hierarchy. Events still bubble correctly through your component tree. Context still flows. The only thing that changes is where the DOM nodes appear in the document."

Focus management in portals

// Use useEffect to trap focus inside the modal when it opens:
const dialogRef = useRef(null);

useEffect(() => {
  if (isOpen) dialogRef.current?.focus();
}, [isOpen]);

// return createPortal(<div ref={dialogRef} tabIndex={-1}>...</div>, document.body);

storyBeats.text: A door in the tower's basement opens into the rooftop — the component renders from one location in the tree but appears at a completely different location in the DOM. 'The React family connection stays,' says Vex. 'Only the DOM address changes.'

storyBeats.speaker: Vex the Interface Weaver
storyBeats.text: Portals solve one specific problem: CSS containment. When a component needs to escape overflow:hidden or a z-index stacking context, render it in body. Context still works. Events still bubble through React. Only the DOM placement changes.

storyBeats.speaker: Simple portal modal

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Build a <PortalModal isOpen onClose children /> component using createPortal:

  • When isOpen is false, render nothing
  • When isOpen is true, render into document.body via portal
  • An overlay (data-testid="overlay") fills the screen; clicking it calls onClose
  • A dialog box (data-testid="dialog") inside — clicking inside does NOT close the modal
  • Render children inside the dialog
  • Show/hide the modal from a parent component with a button

guidedPracticeTests.label: Modal is not rendered when closed
Modal renders when open button clicked

subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Build a reusable <Tooltip text children /> component using a portal. Show the tooltip (rendered in document.body) when the user hovers over the wrapped children. Position it near the mouse using inline styles. Hide on mouse leave. Include an accessible role="tooltip" attribute.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain what a React portal is and why it's needed. Describe the specific CSS problem it solves. Then explain the important behaviour: events still bubble through the React component tree even though the DOM placement is different — why does this matter?

questions.prompt: What is the main problem that React portals solve?
options: CSS containment — rendering UI outside of ancestors with overflow:hidden or z-index constraints
Performance — portals render faster than standard components
State sharing — portals allow components to share state without context
Code splitting — portals lazy-load their content
questions.answer: CSS containment — rendering UI outside of ancestors with overflow:hidden or z-index constraints
questions.explanation: Portals let you escape the CSS stacking context and overflow constraints of ancestor elements. A modal in a card with overflow:hidden would be clipped; rendering it via portal in document.body places it at the top of the DOM, free from those constraints.

questions.prompt: A button inside a portal modal is clicked. Which component tree receives the click event?
options: The React component tree — events bubble through the React hierarchy, not the DOM hierarchy
Only document.body — that's where the portal is mounted
No parent component — portals are isolated from event bubbling
The DOM hierarchy — events bubble through the DOM where the portal is mounted
questions.answer: The React component tree — events bubble through the React hierarchy, not the DOM hierarchy
questions.explanation: React's synthetic event system routes events through the React component tree, not the DOM tree. A click inside a portal bubbles up through the portal's React parent components, even though in the DOM the portal is a direct child of body. This is intentional — it means onClick handlers on the portal's React ancestors still fire.

questions.prompt: When is createPortal the right tool vs. simply using high z-index and position:fixed?
options: When the component is inside a stacking context that cannot be changed — portals escape it; z-index only works within the same stacking context
Always — portals are the correct way to render any floating UI
Only for modals — not tooltips or dropdowns
When the component needs to persist after its React parent unmounts
questions.answer: When the component is inside a stacking context that cannot be changed — portals escape it; z-index only works within the same stacking context
questions.explanation: position:fixed and z-index are often sufficient when you control the entire stacking context. When a component is nested inside a third-party component with its own stacking context (transform, filter, or will-change CSS), z-index won't escape it — a portal will.
